However, in memory-constrained inference settings, expert weights must be offloaded to CPU, creati\n[... excerpt gap ...]\n\n7 Conclusion\n\n\n\n\nMoEs enable scaling to hundreds of billions of parameters via sparse activations (Fedus et al., 2022). Under memory-constrained settings that rely on offloading, inference becomes I/O-bound due to CPU-GPU expert transfers, reducing TPOT. We introduce an inference-time expert prefetching scheme that speculates future expert selection from internal model representations, enabling expert transfers to overlap with computation and improving TPOT. Our parameter-free approach uses the quasi-hidden state to predict next-layer experts over several modern MoE architectures, while a lightweight estimator selectively improves hit rate over high drift layers. Integrated into the YALIS inference engine, our approach achieves up to 5-14% TPOT improvement over on-demand expert loading while largely preserving downstream task accuracy. By reducing the cost incurred by expert offloading, this work makes large open-source MoE models more practical for local deployment on consumer hardware.\n\n\n\n\n8 Future Work\n\n\n\n\nOur analysis of prefetching focused primarily on CPU-GPU expert offloading settings on consumer and single-GPU datacenter hardware. A natural extension is to study more resource-constrained deployments (e.g., smartphones, ro\n[... excerpt gap ...]\n\n Experimental support, please\n view the build logs\n for errors. When a store tile extends past an expert's capacity, it can overwrite valid rows of the next expert. This affects both BF16 and FP8: capacity 32 reproduces it, and capacity 96 also fails when experts are nearly full.\n\nKeep the expert dimension in the output descriptor and reuse the existing 3D TMA store path. This preserves tile selection and the compute pipeline without adding buffers or synchronization. Boundary regressions are integrated into the existing BF16 and FP8 test suites.\n\nThis revisits the limitation discussed in #15 and the small-capacity failure reported in #268. #15 previously fixed small capacities by shrinking the store tile and rejected larger capacities not divisible by the tile size; it also suggested 3D TMA but deferred support for those cases. This change handles both small and non-tile-aligned capacities through the same output path.\n\nOn H200, the median paired latency changes across six rounds were between \u22120.17% and +0.16% for the larger tested shapes. The smallest shape was about 1.9% slower for BF16 and 1.5% slower for FP8, roughly 0.06\u20130.08 \u00b5s. The uniform 3D path avoids maintaining separate aligned and unaligned implementations, at that small measured cost.\n\n<details>\n<summary>Reproduction and validation</summary>\n\nRequires an SM90 GPU and a source build of DeepGEMM. g^(m / (sqrt(g) + 1)) * sigmoid(g) : g * sigmoid(g)   # negative half is SiLU\r\nout      = min(PowLU(gate), limit) * clamp(up, -limit, limit)            # clamp after the activation\r\n```\r\n\r\n- Adds `ActivationType::PowLU = 11` (`InvalidType` \u2192 12) in all three enum copies, the\r\n  serializer, and **both** `isGatedActivation()` predicates \u2014 the CUTLASS copy in\r\n  `moe_gemm_kernels.h` is the one that drives GEMM1's `N = 2\u00b7inter_size` and workspace sizing.\r\n- Implements `PowLUAdaptor` (fp32, element-wise sign branch, `__powf`), wired into\r\n  `doGatedActivation`'s dispatch and `doActivation`'s enum-indexed `fn_list`, which gains a\r\n  bounds check against out-of-range enum values.\r\n- **No `ActivationParams` ABI change**: `m` rides the generic per-expert `swiglu_alpha` slot\r\n  and the post-activation clamp rides `swiglu_limit` \u2014 the same trade `SwigluStepAdaptor`\r\n  makes for its `limit`. GEMM epilogues", "body": "## \ud83d\udccc Description\n\nAdds an optional `delta` input to the PrimsTS dense FP8/NVFP4 GEMMs so callers can fuse an\nadditive per-element update \u2014 typically an unmerged LoRA term `scale \u00b7 (x\u00b7A\u1d40)\u00b7B\u1d40` \u2014 into the\nGEMM epilogue instead of running a separate add (and, for SwiGLU / QKV QK-norm+RoPE, instead\nof falling back to the unfused path).\n\n`delta` is a BF16 `[M, N]` tensor indexed by GEMM column. The epilogue adds it to the\ndequantized FP32 accumulator after weight/activation scales, bias and `qkv_scale`, and before\nthe SwiGLU activation, QK-norm/RoPE, or the output conversion:\n\n- `linear`: `out = bf16(acc_dequant + bias + delta)`\n- `swiglu`: the delta is added to both columns of each interleaved (value, gate) pair before `value * silu(gate)`\n- `qkv_qknorm_rope`: the delta is added before the RMS statistics and before the normalized store, so QK-norm sees the updated Q/K\n\nAPI:\n- New trailing `delta=None` on `fp8_linear`, `fp8_linear_swiglu`, `fp8_qkv_qknorm_rope`, `fp4_linear`, `fp4_linear_swiglu`, `fp4_qkv_qknorm_rope`, and on `PreparedFp4Linear.__call__`.\n- `PrimsTsGemmConfig.has_delta` (default `False`) is a compile-time flag; kernels compiled without it are unchanged. Delta kernels get a `_delta` name suffix and their own autotune cache entry.\n- A prepared NVFP4 projection builds the delta variant lazily on the first call that passes a `delta`, so the same object can be called with and without one.\n\nConstraints (validated in Python, raising `ValueError`): BF16 output only (FP8 output and packed NVFP4 output are rejected), `delta` must be a contiguous, 16-byte aligned `[M, N]` BF16 tensor on the GEMM's device, and `N % 8 == 0`.\n\nImplementation is in `GmemDResource` (`flashinfer/prims_ts/gemm/kernel.py`): one vector add in the main store path, scalar adds in the partial-N tail (gated and non-gated), and one in the QKV QK-norm statistics pass, all behind `const_expr(self.delta is not None)`.\n\n## \ud83d\udd0d Related Issues\n\n<!-- none -->\n\n## \ud83d\ude80 Pull Request Checklist\n\n### \u2705 Pre-commit Checks\n\n- [x] I have installed `pre-commit` by running `pip install pre-commit` (or used your preferred method).\n- [x] I have installed the hooks with `pre-commit install`.\n- [x] I have run the hooks manually with `pre-commit run --all-files` and fixed any reported issues.\n\n## \ud83e\uddea Tests\n\n- [x] Tests have been added or updated as needed.\n- [x] All tests are passing (`unittest`, etc.).\n\nNew tests in `tests/prims_ts/test_gemm_fp8.py` and `tests/prims_ts/test_gemm_fp4.py`:\n- `test_{fp8,fp4}_linear_delta_matches_sum`: result equals the same GEMM without delta plus `delta`; invalid deltas (wrong dtype/shape/alignment, FP8 output) raise. This PR makes `get_humming_moe_gemm_type()` return `indexed` when all of these hold:\n\n- the experts are MXFP4 with DeepSeek V4 routing;\n- `model_type` is `deepseek_v41` or `deepseek_v41_text`;\n- the device is CUDA SM90;\n- there are no all2all kernels, or the backend is `allgather_reducescatter`.\n\nWithout EP, Humming already picks indexed, so nothing changes there. `VLLM_HUMMING_MOE_GEMM_TYPE` still overrides the choice. Since #56997, Humming is the default MXFP4 MoE backend on SM90, so V4.1 with EP on Hopper otherwise runs the grouped GEMM by default; this PR moves that default path to indexed too. The rule applies with BF16 activations and with per-token FP8 activations (`--quantization-config.moe.activation fp8_per_token`).\n\nThe MXFP4 MoE method (DeepSeek V4/V4.1, Kimi-K3, plain mxfp4) now runs `quantization_config.moe.activation`:\n\n```bash\nvllm serve deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash -tp 8 --enable-expert-parallel \\\n    --moe-backend humming --quantization-config.moe.activation fp8_per_token\n```\n\n- Humming takes the named format as a fixed input schema, with its input-schema fallback off.\n- Other explicit backends must run the named format, and `auto` keeps only the backends that do. Before, these models ignored the name on every backend. Now a backend that does not run it stops vLLM, on every platform (CUDA, ROCm, XPU, CPU). The DeepSeek V4 MegaMoE backends (`deep_gemm_mega_moe`, `aiter_mega_moe`) build their own experts and do not read the name. On ROCm, the Kimi-K3 AITER path, which skips the backend selector, now refuses a named activation instead of ignoring it. For example, `fp8_per_token` with `flashinfer_trtllm` now stops vLLM instead of running MXFP8. A draft model with its own `speculative_config.moe_backend` inherits the target's `quantization_config`, so the same rule applies to it.\n- The startup log prints the format Humming runs: `Humming MoE activations: fp8_per_token (group size 0, scale dtype float32)`. The line appears for every Humming MoE model, gpt-oss included.\n- On SM90 Humming, `mxfp8` and `fp8_per_block_dynamic` stop vLLM at startup, before the weights load. Humming has no e8m0 input scales on WGMMA, and humming 0.1.16 rejects fp32 group scales with MXFP4 weights (#60600). Group-wise scales are also 1.2x to 24x slower than per-token in the SM90 Humming GEMM at M >= 256 (numbers in the review reply).\n- `VLLM_HUMMING_INPUT_QUANT_CONFIG` still works as on main, with no early check: a format Humming cannot run fails while the weights convert, as before. With `--moe-backend humming`, setting it together with `moe.activation` is an error.\n- gpt-oss is unchanged. With no name, nothing changes.\n\n## Test Plan\n\n```bash\npytest tests/kernels/moe/test_moe.py -k \"named_activation or activation_on_sm90 or humming or indexed\"\npytest tests/quantization/test_quantization_config_args.py \\\n    tests/quantization/test_humming_mxfp4_block_fp8.py tests/kernels/moe/test_b12x.py \\\n    tests/kernels/moe/test_topk_softplus_sqrt.py tests/quantization/test_gfx950_moe.py\npytest tests/models/kimi_k3/test_gfx942_int4.py\npytest tests/kernels/moe/test_ocp_mx_moe.py -k unsupported_reasons\n```\n\n`test_humming_deepseek_v41_hopper_uses_indexed_gemm_with_ep` calls `get_humming_moe_gemm_type` and checks that V4.1 with EP gets indexed, with and without `allgather_reducescatter`, and that DeepEP, SM100 and DeepSeek V4 keep the grouped GEMM. It does not need the humming package.\n\n`test_deepseek_v4_mxfp4_backend_must_run_named_activation` checks on any GPU that `auto` and `flashinfer_trtllm` refuse `fp8_per_token`, and that `humming` refuses the env JSON plus a name (\"not both\"). `test_humming_deepseek_v4_activation_on_sm90` checks that SM90 Humming accepts `fp8_per_token` and refuses `mxfp8`. It skips on other GPUs, so in CI it runs only in the optional H100 FP8 MoE kernels job; `kernels-moe-test` runs on L4. The Kimi-K3 AITER refusal has no unit test: it is a short guard, and a test would have to mock the whole K3 path.\n\n`user_moe_activation_override()` (was `_user_moe_activation_override()`) is now runtime covering routing metadata preparation, input\r\n  permutation and quantization, GEMM1, SwiGLU, requantization, GEMM2, output\r\n  permutation, router weighting, and top-k reduction.\r\n- Add cross-backend consistency against FlashInfer.\r\n\r\nThe backend is selected with:\r\n\r\n```bash\r\n--moe-runner-backend cutlass\r\n```\r\n\r\n### Execution participant W as MXFP4 weights\r\n    participant Y as MoE output\r\n\r\n    X->>R: tokens and topk=6\r\n    W-->>S: Humming-compatible view\r\n    W-->>F: Humming view\r\n    par SGLang EP1 path\r\n        R->>S: GPU-built routing metadata\r\n        S->>S: reorder + per-token FP8 quant\r\n        S->>S: grouped GEMM1\r\n        S->>S: SwiGLU + FP8 requant\r\n        S->>S: grouped GEMM2\r\n        S-->>Y: reorder + router-weight reduction\r\n    and FlashInfer\r\n        R->>F: topk IDs + router weights\r\n        F->>F: bucketed tactic lookup\r\n        F->>F: fused MoE body\r\n        F-->>Y: fused finalize\r\n    end\r\n    Note over S,F: Same logical MXFP4 weights and routing inputs<br/>Different runtime orchestration and scheduling\r\n```\r\n\r\n## Implementation\r\n\r\n### MXFP4A8 tensor-core path\r\n\r\nWeights remain in checkpoint-native MXFP4. Activations are quantized per token\r\nto FP8 E4M3. The E2M1 values\r\n`{0, 0.5, 1, 1.5, 2, 3, 4, 6}` are exactly representable in E4M3, so the\r\nE2M1-to-E4M3 conversion uses a lossless signed-nibble lookup.\r\n\r\nThe mixed-input mainloop derives the scale group from\r\n`TileK / PackedScalesNum`, allowing the existing INT4A8 group-128 path and the\r\nnew MXFP4A8 group-32 path to share the same mainloop without changing INT4\r\nbehavior.\r\n\r\n### Load-time weight preprocessing\r\n\r\nThe EP1 path prepares one runtime representation after checkpoint loading:\r\n\r\n- interleaved MXFP4 weights;\r\n- folded E8M0 offsets;\r\n- one residual scale per expert.\r\n\r\nThe representation follows the SM90 Humming preprocessing semantics. Runtime\r\nexecution is implemented by SGLang AOT kernels.\r\n\r\nOnly the fused representation is retained for EP1 to avoid storing two complete\r\nweight layouts on H20.\r\n\r\n### Fused EP1 execution\r\n\r\n`cutlass_mxfp4a8_fused_moe_core` performs:\r\n\r\n1. expert-offset, problem-size, and permutation preparation;\r\n2. routed-input reorder and per-token FP8 quantization;\r\n3. grouped GEMM1;\r\n4. fused SwiGLU, optional clamp, and FP8 requantization;\r\n5. grouped GEMM2;\r\n6. output reorder, FP32 router-weight multiplication,\r\n   `routed_scaling_factor`, and top-k reduction.\r\n\r\nFor `M <= 64`, metadata preparation and shuffled input quantization use a\r\nbounded fused CUDA path. Larger batches use the AOT metadata and quantization\r\nkernels without host synchronization. Intermediate tensors are retained in\r\nreusable workspaces.\r\n\r\n### SM90 scheduling\r\n\r\nThe implementation includes:\r\n\r\n- a persistent single-warpgroup ping-pong kernel for tiny and arbitrary\r\n  serving-time shapes;\r\n- a precomputed grouped scheduler with prebuilt TMA descriptors for validated\r\n  large-M buckets;\r\n- a packed warp-shuffle GEMM2 epilogue.\r\n\r\n| Tokens | It contained 22 files mixing norms, routing, GEMMs, collectives and reductions, with no KernelSpecs and no kernel tests. It had been added to `_GROUPS`, which is the only thing the guard test checked, so the test did not catch it.\n- `attention/dsv4/` and `attention/dsa/` had collected quantization kernels, KV-cache stores and copies, a split-K GEMV, collective attention-residual kernels, runtime controllers and config predicates, and test oracles.\n- Elsewhere, ops sat in the wrong group: GEMMs in `quantization`, RMSNorms in `elementwise`, attention metadata in `kvcache`, a forwarding shim in `attention/utils.py`, and the same computation implemented in two or three groups.\n\nThis PR fixes all of it in one pass. It writes the classification rules into the README and the `kernel-organization` skill, and makes the guard test enforce the README.\n\n## Classification rules (README + skill)\n\n- RoPE, including standalone RoPE and position ids, stays in `attention`.\n- **Producer + output quantization belongs to the producer's group:**\n  - norm + quant \u2192 `layernorm`\n  - activation + quant \u2192 `activation`\n  - a GEMM with a quant epilogue \u2192 `gemm`\n  - MoE dispatch + quant \u2192 `moe`\n  - `quantization` holds only pure format conversion: quant, dequant, scale layout, repack.\n- **Any kernel that performs a cross-rank collective, or reads or writes peer memory, \u2192 `communication`**, whatever compute it fuses. Workspaces, symmetric buffers and process groups stay in `srt/layers/communication/`.\n- **`kvcache` owns ops that read or write KV-cache contents:** store, gather, copy, quantize-into-cache, clear rows.\n- **`attention` owns the index, shape and schedule tables attention kernels consume:** page tables, cu_seqlens, kv_indices, schedule metadata.\n- A fused compute+store op stays with its compute group.\n- `kda_kernels/` and `cake_kernels/` are documented as the agent-generated kernel backends. They are deliberately left in place, and new agent kernels keep landing there.\n\n**Guard test** (`test_kernels_namespace.py`):\n- The README group list must equal `_GROUPS`.\n- The README Layout must list exactly the packages under `sglang/kernels/`.\n\nBoth checks fail on main.\n\n## Modifications\n\nAll relocations are `git mv` plus import updates. Every moved function, class and constant was checked to be byte-identical apart from import paths, either by AST comparison or by a normalized diff. Relocation commits are kept apart from semantic commits. No forwarding shims remain: 94 old module paths have zero references anywhere.\n\n### `ops/muse_spark` dissolved\n- **layernorm:** `muse_spark_norm_gate{,_jit,_helion}`, `muse_spark_norm_residual{,_jit}`, `muse_spark_rmsnorm_nvfp4_quant{,_helion}`, `_muse_spark_tuning`.\n- **attention:** `muse_spark_qk_norm_rope_store{,_helion}`.\n- **moe:** `muse_spark_routing{,_jit}`, `muse_spark_post_expert_finalize_triton`.\n- **communication:**\n  - `muse_spark_all_gather`, `muse_spark_all_gather_norm_residual`\n  - `muse_spark_moe_finalize_all_reduce{,_cutedsl,_helion}`\n  - SP `cutlass_all_gather_gemm`, `cutlass_gemm_reduce_scatter`, `sp_collective_gemm` (moved from `gemm`)\n- **elementwise:** `row_sum`. **gemm:** `muse_spark_router_gemm`. It is kept but still unused; the model only reads its `MAX_TOKENS` threshold.\n- **Helion runtime:** \u2192 `kernels/jit/utils/helion_runtime.py`.\n- **Runtime state \u2192 `srt/layers/communication/`:** the GEMM+all-gather composition and projection workspace, `FinalizePushWorkspace`, and the SP collective-GEMM symmetric-memory workspace. The SP kernels now take the workspace as an argument.\n- **The model calls the all-gather+norm op directly.** The removed `forward_with_ag` used to route it, and the norm op no longer imports srt model classes.\n- **New coverage:** KernelSpecs for every entry point, plus 6 kernel test files (fused vs native). `triton_sum` \u2192 `sglang.test.kernels`, used as the `row_sum` bitwise In batched\nprocessing, QKV generation and feed-forward networks involve compute-intensive\nmatrix-matrix multiplications (GEMM), while multi-head attention requires\nbandwidth-heavy matrix-vector multiplications (GEMV). Conversely, Processing-in-Memory (PIM)\ntechnology is tailored for efficient GEMV computation, while it lacks the\ncomputational power to handle GEMM effectively. Inspired by this insight, we\npropose NeuPIMs, a heterogeneous acceleration system that jointly exploits a\nconventional GEMM-focused NPU and GEMV-optimized PIM devices. The main\nchallenge in efficiently integrating NPU and PIM lies in enabling concurrent\noperations on both platforms, each addressing a specific kernel type. First,\nexisting PIMs typically operate in a \"blocked\" mode, allowing only either NPU\nor PIM to be active at any given time. GitHub", "body": "Conversation\nusernamehaha2022\ncommented\nJul 22, 2026\n\u2022\nedited\nLoading\nUh oh!\nThere was an error while loading.\nPlease reload this page\n.\nCopy link\nCopy Markdown\nSummary\nThis PR pipelines direct NVLink dispatch using three shared-memory TMA buffers per dispatch warp.\nPreviously, a dispatch warp prepared tokens sequentially around remote S2G stores. With this change, the next token's hidden data, scale factors, metadata, and routing information are prefetched while previous remote stores remain in flight.\nAt steady state, the three buffers are used for:\nA previous token whose remote S2G store may still be in flight.\nThe current token being sent to remote ranks.\nThe next token being prefetched from global memory.\nBefore recycling the oldest buffer,\ntma_store_wait<1>()\nreduces the number of outstanding store groups to one. This keeps buffer reuse safe without fully draining all remote stores between tokens.\nThe shared-memory calculation now accounts for all three staging buffers, and direct NVLink dispatch is limited to at most 14 dispatch warps. SM89 is the first architecture below Hopper that has FP8 Tensor Cores.\n\nPreviously, SM80 and SM89 used the same path. The path required SM90 or higher for FP8. This was correct for SM80 because Ampere has no FP8 Tensor Cores. It was wrong for SM89. SM89 implements the instruction `mma.sync.aligned.m16n8k32.row.col.f32.e4m3.e4m3.f32` (`QMMA.16832.F32.E4M3.E4M3`). The change separates the two architectures and gives SM89 a real kernel.\n\n## Why\n\n- SM89 has FP8 Tensor Cores. It does not have the SM90 features (no TMA, no `mbarrier.try_wait.parity`, no WGMMA, no clusters). It could not reuse the SM90 or SM100 kernels. It fell back to BF16 through cuBLASLt.\n- FP8 users on Ada had to dequantize and run BF16. They lost about 2\u00d7 of Tensor Core throughput.\n- The shared SM80/SM89 path also gave wrong error messages. An SM89 user saw a message that did not apply to their GPU.\n\n## Design\n\nSM89 has no TMA and no asynchronous barriers. The kernel uses the pre-Hopper primitives.\n\n- It uses `mma.sync` (wrapped in `deep_gemm/mma/sm89.cuh`, with A/B/C fragment layouts documented) and `ldmatrix.x4` for operand staging.\n- It uses a multi-stage `cp.async` pipeline with a 128-byte XOR swizzle.\n- It uses a persistent block scheduler (one CTA per SM). Tiles walk in a loop.\n- It uses direct global stores because SM89 has no TMA store. It has an alignment-safe scalar tail. An MMA lane owns a pair of adjacent columns. For odd N the element offset of a row can be odd. A 2-element vector store is then illegal. This caused the original misaligned address failure.\n- Block K is fixed at 128 because of the per-128-channel scaling granularity. Pipeline depth and tile shapes come from a new cost model in `csrc/jit_kernels/heuristics/sm89.hpp`. The warp split uses one shared function `get_mma_sync_warps_n()`. Host heuristics and device code both call it so they cannot disagree.\n\nBoth SM90 SF recipes are supported:  \n`(1, 1, 128)` (per-token A and B scales) and  \n`(1, 128, 128)` (per-token A, one B scale per 128-column N block).  \nThe second recipe is the default when FP32 scales are used. SM89 uses the same FP32 SF layouts as SM90. The function `transform_sf_into_required_layout` was extended. It was not duplicated.\n\n## Scope\n\nSupported features:  \ndense FP8 GEMM, K-major (NT) operands only, FP32 and BF16 outputs, `D = C + A @ B`, ragged M/N, `k % 16 == 0`, both aliases (`fp8_fp4_gemm_nt`, `fp8_gemm_nt`, `fp4_gemm_nt`), and shape specialization.\n\nStill rejected (with an explicit message that names the requirement):  \ngrouped and K-grouped FP8, MN-major FP8 operands, FP4, custom epilogues, `alpha` scaling, PDL, and MQA/attention.  \nBF16 keeps its cuBLASLt fallback.\n\n## Incidental fixes\n\n- `set_pdl()` now panics below SM90. It no longer sets a flag that `griddepcontrol` cannot honour.  \n  `cudaGridDependencySynchronize()` is wrapped in a no-op below `__CUDA_ARCH__ >= 900` so the SF-layout kernels compile for SM89.\n- `call_cublaslt_api` used `CUBLAS_COMPUTE_32F_FAST_TF32` for non-FP32 operands. That mode only down-casts FP32 inputs to TF32. BF16/FP8 operands ran at TF32 precision by mistake. Now only FP32 inputs use that mode.\n- A new `DG_PANIC` macro throws always and carries a message.\n\n## Bug found during validation\n\nThe persistent loop primed its `cp.async` pipeline only in the prologue before the tile loop. It relied on a cross-tile tail load to prime the next tile. A tile\u2019s tail can only reach the stages that are already free of the current tile \u2014 prologue stages `p \u2208 [0, kNumStages-2-num_k_blocks]`. The next tile\u2019s K loop consumes `p = 0..num_k_blocks-1`. When `num_k_blocks < kNumStages-1` (example: `k=512`, 4 blocks, 8 stages) the high stages were never reloaded. The next tile read the previous tile\u2019s shared memory. Symptom: non-deterministic `nan` and values near 1e30. The problem appeared only for small M spread over many N tiles.\n\nThe fix extracts the prologue into `prime_pipeline()` and re-primes unconditionally after the epilogue. The re-prime is guarded by `cp_async_wait<0>()` and a `__syncthreads()`. `cp.async` completion is per-thread, so both are required before the stages can be reused. The change removes a prologue/epilogue overlap that was never correct. Meanwhile\nx + |x|\ncompiles to a single FADD with the absolute-value operand modifier, which is a free encoding bit in the instruction word:\nFADD R3, R3, |R3|    ; one instruction, full rate (cuobjdump, sm_90a)\nThe relu executes once per\n(token, head, kv)\nscore element in the MQA logits epilogue, so at 64 vs 128 ops/clk/SM the FMNMX form doubles the FP32 pipe time spent on relu alone.\nSince\nx + |x| = 2 \u00b7 relu(x)\nholds exactly for all finite IEEE-754 floats (\n+0\nfor x \u2264 0), the doubled sum is simply halved by folding\n* 0.5f\ninto the already-existing\nscale_kv\nmultiplication (an exponent decrement, also exact):\n//\nBefore:\nreturn\nfmaxf(shifted_accum[j],\n0\n) * weights[i][(j /\n4\n) *\n2\n+ (j &\n1\n)];\n...\nfloat\nv_0 = (sum[\n0\n] + sum[\n1\n]) * scale_kv_0;\n//\nAfter:\nreturn\n(shifted_accum[j] + fabsf(shifted_accum[j])) * weights[i][(j /\n4\n) *\n2\n+ (j &\n1\n)];\n...\nfloat\nv_0 = (sum[\n0\n] + sum[\n1\n]) * (scale_kv_0 *\n0\n.\n5f\n);\nThe same technique is already used by the SM100 kernel (\nsm100_mqa_logits.cuh\n, packed\nFADD2\nvariant); this PR brings it to SM90. E4M3 covering\nthe full 512-wide K (rope lanes quantized, no BF16 rope segment) plus a 16B\nfooter of 16 UE8M0 scales over 32-wide groups (the\ndeepseek-ai/FlashMLA#221\nlayout, SM100-only there). Add ModelType::DSV4_1 on top of the ScaleSpec\ngroundwork: GLM53_NOPE-style geometry (D_ROPE=0) composed with a 32-wide\nUE8M0 footer.\n\nKernel side the format is simpler than DSV4 (one 512B bulk per row, a single\nunified block-scaled FP8 QK pass, no rope MMA paths). The two new mechanics:\n\n- the 16B footer row generalizes the scale gather from one uint64_t to a\n  width-selected load (uint4) in both the prefill IO helper and the decode\n  kernel's staged gather;\n- the 32-wide groups constrain the XV W-fold (one scale group per W buffer),\n  so an 8-warp XV split would floor NT_PER_WARP_XV to 0: decode runs a\n  4-math-warp tile at BI=64 (the DOTS3_SWA halving precedent) and prefill is\n  SG-only on the BI=32 producer/consumer tile. The ComputeTraits/SmemLayout\n  aliases now take the XV warp count so the NT_PER_WARP_XV assert evaluates at\n  the warp count the XV MMA actually runs at.\n\nSelection is explicit everywhere (d_qk=512 collides with DSV4, the 528B\npayload with GLM53_NOPE): the functional API gains kv_scale_format=\n\"ue8m0_g32\", the TRTLLM-compat entry kv_cache_format=\"fp8_dsv41\", and the\ndecode-dsv4 FFI takes an explicit model_type (-1 keeps the legacy width\ninference, matching the paged-entry kAuto convention). Dual-cache decode is\nsupported like DSV4; dual-cache prefill (MG_DUAL) is intentionally not\ninstantiated. The scale must be re-applied to the dequantized FC1 output **before** the clamp / SwiGLU nonlinearity, i.e. inside the FC1 epilogue. This PR ports that feature from the kernel team's MR (`cutedsl_megamoe!1`, \"support static runtime per-token global scale\") into the vendored drop and plumbs it through the shim, the FI backend, and `MoEEpTensors`.\n\n**Math.** With `s_t` the per-token scale and `q(\u00b7)` the host NVFP4 quantizer:\n\n```\nkernel input:   q(x_t / s_t)\nFC1:            acc1_t = W1 \u00b7 q(x_t / s_t)             \u2248 (W1 x_t) / s_t\nFC1 epilogue:   real   = fc1_alpha_e \u00b7 s_t \u00b7 acc1_t  \u2192 clamp \u2192 gated act (\u2192 \u00d7 topk) \u2192 NVFP4 quant\nFC2 / combine:  unchanged\n```\n\n**What changes**\n\n- Kernel drop (`kernel_src/sm100/cutedsl_megamoe/src/`, recorded as a pending-upstream diff in `VENDOR.md`):\n  - `kernel_fc12.py` / `megamoe_kernel.py`: new constructor switch `enable_fc1_activation_per_token_scale` (enters `name()`), new optional runtime arg `fc1_activation_per_token_scale: (T,) fp32`, new pool-ordered local workspace region `l1_fc1_activation_per_token_scale_buffer`. Tokens 32..63 are activated after the register transpose (one token per lane \u2192 one scale per lane); tokens 0..31 are activated *before* the transpose, where register `i` of lane `L` holds token `2i + (L//2)%2`, so the scale is fetched with `shfl.idx` from lane `2i + parity` (16 SHFL per lane per subtile). That is the pattern CUTLASS uses (`fence_view_async_shared()`, then the barrier, then the async-proxy read).\n\n#### Why the fence is needed\n\nPTX ISA 9.4, \u00a79.7.17.7.1, the `wgmma.fence` page; \u00a79.7.15.7.1 in ISA 8.8:\n\n> An async proxy fence must be used to establish an ordering between prior writes to shared memory matrices and subsequent reads of the same matrices in a wgmma.mma_async instruction.\n\n- `wgmma` reads shared memory through the async proxy.\n- `__syncthreads()` synchronizes the threads but does not by itself order generic-proxy stores before async-proxy reads; PTX requires a proxy fence for that.\n- `wgmma_fence()` (`wgmma.fence`) orders register accesses, not shared memory.\n\n#### Cost\n\nOne fence per thread per launch.\n\n#### Testing\n\n- Evidence: found by reading the compiled PTX against the ISA. The first `wgmma` read comes after two barriers and a weight TMA, so the window is likely closed in practice today. AITER's 2-stage CK fp8 MoE GEMM is numerically broken for non-128-aligned intermediate sizes (Gemma4-26B-A4B: 704), so #53259 rounds the size up to 768 for the AITER backend. Its comment claims the padded tail is zeroed by the loader \u2014 it is not: `create_weights` allocates `w13_weight`/`w2_weight` with `torch.empty` and the loader only narrow-copies the checkpoint's real 704 rows/columns. Rows 704\u2013767 of `w13` (gate/up) and columns 704\u2013767 of `w2` keep whatever the caching allocator hands out \u2014 device memory freed earlier in the same process \u2014 and that is live weight for the kernel: non-zero pad activations after GELU pollute the per-token `a2` quant scale and leak through the `w2` tail into the layer output.\n\n## How this shows up\n\nWhether a given process gets harmful leftovers in the padding depends on the allocation order at load time, so most processes look fine and an occasional one produces sporadically implausible tokens (typo-like output) with no error or warning. A load-time probe of the padded region in fresh processes finds non-zero bytes there; deliberately filling one layer's padding with stale-weight-like bytes reproduces the symptom, and filling every layer collapses the model. Zero-allocating removes the effect.\n\nThe other users of `maybe_roundup_sizes` (mxfp4, quark nvfp4) already allocate with `torch.zeros`; this makes the fp8 methods do the same and corrects the comment. The memset is a one-time cost at load.\n\n## Test Plan\n\n- Unit tests from #53259 (`test_fp8_round_up_intermediate_size_for_aiter`, `test_activation_method_enum_values`, The frontend is NUMA-bound.\n\nSGLang patches (`configs/dsv41flash-sglang-patches.sh` applies `configs/dsv41flash-sglang-patches/*.patch` to `/sgl-workspace/sglang`, which is the image's editable install; it uses `git apply`, is idempotent, holds a lock across workers on the same node, and fails the worker if any hunk does not apply):\n\n| Patch | Upstream | Fixes |\n|---|---|---|\n| `sglang-pr44623.patch` | sgl-project/sglang#44623 (open) | Lets the external cache linker register DeepSeek-V4.1's hybrid KV pools (pool assemblers, unified linker, Mooncake/UMBP direct linkers) |\n\nDrop the patch once the pinned image contains it. CUDA graph replay", "body": "A CUDA graph kernel node keeps the same `%gridid` on every replay. The `mega_mhc` split barriers tag executions with `%gridid`, so after a replay a barrier line still holds `encode_state(grid_idx, kNumSplits)` \u2014 exactly what the next replay waits for. A Mix or Norm waiter whose m-block init CTA has not started yet proceeds at once and reads the previous replay's split partials (the graph-pool scratch is the same memory). `wait_init` only protects producers.\n\nThis tags each execution with an epoch instead of `%gridid`. The epoch and an exit count live in the unused tail of the first barrier line, so the host-side barrier buffer and the compiled extension are unchanged (JIT headers only). issue\nCopy link\nNew issue\nCopy link\nOpen\nOpen\n[Bug] non-deterministic results in sm90 tf32_hc_prenorm_gemm\n#449\nCopy link\nDescription\nleevan\nopened\non Sep 16, 2026\nIssue body actions\nDescription\nOn SM90 GPUs, tf32_hc_prenorm_gemm can produce incorrect and non-deterministic GEMM outputs when processing multiple K blocks.\nRepeated calls with identical inputs can return different results.\nRoot cause\nThe kernel uses asynchronous WGMMA instructions with register-source A operands. Previously, the next iteration loaded its A fragment\nbefore waiting for the preceding iteration's WGMMA to complete. This could overwrite A registers while they were still being read by\nthe in-flight WGMMA.\nFix\nProposed fix:\n#448\nThe fix moves\nwarpgroup_wait<0>()\nimmediately after\nwarpgroup_commit_batch()\n, ensuring that each iteration's WGMMA completes\nbefore its A registers are reused.\nThe PR also adds a regression test covering split-K, PDL enabled/disabled, and default/side streams. It checks outputs against FP32\nreferences and verifies repeatability across identical launches.\nValidation\nWith the fix applied, both the existing hyperconnection tests and all 24 configurations of the new regression test passed on an SM90\nGPU.\nTODO\nfix will introduce some performance regression which suppose to be mitigated in upcoming PRs\u3002\nReactions are currently unavailable\nActivity\nLiRunGuo\ncommented\non\nSep 22, 2026\nLiRunGuo\non Sep 22, 2026\nMore actions\nI measured this on an H200 (SM90, driver 580.159.03, PyTorch 2.11.0+cu130) with DeepGEMM\nmain\n(\n78b6900\n), in case it helps the review of\n#448\n.\nReproduction.\nI ran the 24 shapes from\ntest_hc_prenorm_gemm\n(\nm\nin 13 / 137 / 4096 / 8192,\nn = 24\n,\nk\nin 7168 / 7680 / 28672, with and without 16 splits), with 50 back-to-back launches per shape. It looks for writes to the A registers of an in-flight\nHGMMA\ngroup before the\nWARPGROUP.DEPBAR\nthat waits for it, and found none: ptxas puts the A fragments of consecutive stages in different registers. So the source-level race is real, but these two ptxas versions do not turn it into a hazard for these instantiations. The same model text therefore produces different response content when a backend changes only its chunk boundaries.\r\n\r\nOn unmodified `8cadfede7063c896b944e7bae05daa3549ae97ea`, the new test fails when the JSON prefix is split after its first character: the split stream produces two leading spaces while the single-chunk stream produces one. The op is the pre-finalize step of a manifold-constrained hyper-connection (mHC) boundary with `HC = 4` residual streams. It also fuses the next sublayer's RMSNorm into its output.\n\nOn SM100 / SM103, decode batches run a new thread-block-cluster kernel. Every other call runs a composable fp32 PyTorch implementation of the same contract, so the API always returns a result.\n\n### Model and use case\n\n- **Model:** the op was written for decode of [GLM-5.3-Flash](https://huggingface.co/RedHatAI/GLM-5.3-Flash-NVFP4) (hidden size 4096, `hc_mult = 4`, 45 layers) on GB300.\n- **Call count:** every attention and every MoE sublayer is wrapped by an mHC boundary, so the op runs **90 times per decode step**.\n- **Current vLLM path:** for batches of up to 32 tokens, vLLM runs each boundary as two kernels:\n  1. `mhc_fused` mixes the sublayer output back into the 4 residual streams and computes split-K partials of the 24 mix logits.\n  2. A **pre-finalize** kernel, written in TileLang. It runs one 96-thread CTA per token, so a decode token's whole pre-finalize runs on a single SM.\n- **This PR** implements step 2.\n\n```mermaid\nflowchart LR\n    B[\"sublayer output<br/>(attention or MoE)\"] --> F[\"mhc_fused<br/>mix into the 4 residual streams<br/>+ split-K partials of the 24 mix logits\"]\n    F -->|\"gemm_out_mul [NS, T, 24] fp32<br/>gemm_out_sqrsum [NS, T] fp32<br/>residual [T, 4, 4096] bf16\"| P[\"<b>mhc_pre_big_fuse_with_norm</b><br/>(this PR)\"]\n    P -->|\"layer_input [T, 4096] bf16<br/>(already RMSNorm'd)\"| N[\"next sublayer<br/>(attention or MoE)\"]\n    P -->|\"post_mix [T, 4]<br/>comb_mix [T, 4, 4]\"| F2[\"next boundary's<br/>mhc_fused\"]\n    N --> F2\n```\n\n### What is fused\n\n```mermaid\nflowchart TB\n    subgraph BEFORE[\"Before: stable FlashInfer APIs, two kernels\"]\n        direction LR\n        A1[\"split-K partials<br/>+ residual\"] --> K1[\"<b>mhc_pre_big_fuse</b><br/>reduce logits \u2192 sigmoids<br/>\u2192 Sinkhorn \u2192   end\n    subgraph AFTER[\"After: this PR, one kernel\"]\n        direction LR\n        A2[\"split-K partials<br/>+ residual + norm_weight\"] --> K3[\"<b>mhc_pre_big_fuse_with_norm</b><br/>reduce logits \u2192 sigmoids \u2192 Sinkhorn<br/>\u2192 weighted sum \u2192 RMSNorm\"]\n        K3 --> O2[\"layer_input\"]\n        K3 --> M2[\"post_mix, comb_mix\"]\n    end\n    BEFORE ~~~ AFTER\n```\n\n| step | computes |\n|---|---|\n| 1. reduce partials | `mixes = \u03a3_s gemm_out_mul[s] \u00b7 rsqrt(\u03a3_s gemm_out_sqrsum[s] / (4\u00b7H) + rms_eps)` |\n| 2. pre | `pre = 20-iteration Sinkhorn of `softmax(mixes[8:24] as 4\u00d74) + hc_sinkhorn_eps` |\n| 5. weighted sum | `ol = \u03a3_j pre[j] \u00b7 residual[:, j, :]` (fp32) |\n| **6. RMSNorm (newly fused)** | `layer_input = bf16(bf16(ol) \u00b7 rsqrt(mean(ol\u00b2) + norm_eps) \u00b7 norm_weight)` |\n\n- Fusing the RMSNorm removes one launch and the `[T, 4096]` bf16 round trip through HBM (8 KB written and read back per token). The RMS statistic is taken on the fp32 sum `ol` rather than on its bf16 copy.\n- vLLM's current TileLang kernel already fuses the same six steps, but on one CTA per token. The speedups under Performance are measured against that kernel, so they come from the cluster design below, not from removing a launch.\n- Per token the op reads 32 KB of residual and writes 8 KB. It is latency-bound, not bandwidth-bound: on one CTA, the 20-iteration Sinkhorn chain, the 4096-wide weighted sum and the RMSNorm reduction run one after another.\n\n### Kernel design This PR moves those missing compilations to startup without changing the kernel math or split-K heuristic.\n\nAddresses #60536. Depends on https://github.com/vllm-project/DeepGEMM/pull/29 for the compile-only entry point used by this implementation.\n\n## Claims\n\n- Register every reachable DeepGEMM mHC pre-norm specialization for GLM's configured token range, deduplicated by `(N, K, num_splits)`.\n- Compile them through the existing startup warmup registry, without allocating input tensors or launching dummy kernels.\n- Keep runtime split selection, kernel math, and backend selection unchanged.\n\n## Details\n\n### Why startup misses these kernels\n\nThe mHC pre-norm path contains a matrix multiplication implemented by DeepGEMM. It selects a split-K count (how many pieces to divide the reduction into) based on the number of tokens in the current engine step. Each distinct split count requires a separately compiled kernel. The row count `M` itself is dynamic, so there is no need to compile once per prompt length.\n\nThe existing selection is:\n\n```python\nnum_splits = max(1, min(num_sms // ceil(M / 64), ceil(K / 64) // 4))\n```\n\nHere `M` is the step's token count, `K` is the input width, and `N` is the output width. For example, with 78 SMs and `K=16384`, `M=64`, `192`, and `16384` select 64, 26, and 1 splits respectively. Compiling the first and last does not compile the middle one. The number of required specializations depends on the GPU and configured token range; the issue's count of missing variants is not a universal constant.\n\nThe startup profile run and CUDA-graph capture exercise only some split counts. GLM does not register the remaining DeepGEMM variants for explicit warmup. The first real request that reaches a missing split therefore compiles it while serving, delaying that engine step and potentially other in-flight requests. This is a JIT coverage gap, not evidence of incorrect model arithmetic.\n\n```text\nBefore: startup warms some splits -> request reaches a new split -> compile -> run\nAfter:  startup warms all reachable splits -> request -> reuse compiled kernel\n```\n\n### What this changes\n\nWhen GLM selects the DeepGEMM path, register its projection dimensions with a small kernel wrapper. The wrapper enumerates token counts up to `max_num_batched_tokens` at the heuristic's 64-token boundaries, maps them to `(N, K, num_splits)`, and deduplicates the keys. Startup compiles those keys; requests continue to call the same DeepGEMM runtime kernel.\n\n### Why a companion DeepGEMM change?\n\nThe first proposal in #60536 is to warm each reachable split by executing one dummy row through the existing API. That can trigger compilation **without changing DeepGEMM**. This PR uses the same coverage strategy, but chooses compile-only warmup to follow the [current warmup contract](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/main/docs/contributing/jit_kernel_warmup.md), which excludes real tensor allocation and dummy kernel launches.\n\nThe companion PR exposes `compile_tf32_hc_prenorm_gemm(n, k, num_splits)`, reusing the runtime JIT source and cache keys but stopping before launch. The trade-off is a cross-repository dependency and additional cold-start compilation time, rather than pauses during requests. This dependency is a choice of implementation, not a requirement inherent to fixing the issue.\n\n### Relationship to earlier work\n\nThis builds on existing warmup work; the idea of warming mHC or DeepGEMM specializations is not new. The remaining gap is **GLM's DeepGEMM pre-norm GEMM with its existing token-dependent split heuristic**.\n\nStatus checked on 2026-10-08:\n\n| Earlier work | Status | What it covers | Why it does not already complete this fix |\n| --- | --- | --- | --- |\n| #50178, Roberto L. This replaces three launches with one, preserves the BF16 boundaries, and retains coefficient overlap. The kernel reuses the existing MNNVL workspace without an additional persistent communication allocation.\n\nEnabled by default for eligible SM100 TP4 forwards with 1\u201316 tokens, including speculative decoding. The selector requires hidden size 5120, hc_mult=4, EP disabled, and a multicast workspace; it does not restrict DP/PP size, LoRA, or attention backend. The existing overlap-support checks still apply, including disabling overlap for ubatching. Larger batches and graph boundaries use the existing operations. Sixteen is the largest size with a validated gain, not a measured crossover.\n\nBuilds on #57603, now merged into main, which overlaps coefficient computation but does not fuse collectives. This differs from #51244's terminal mHC/head fusion. Open-PR searches for `mhc allreduce` and `mhc fusion` found no duplicate of this decoder-boundary collective fusion.\n\nThe independent startup warmup fixes have been extracted: DeepGEMM mHC projection coverage is in #57843, and cached FlashInfer MXFP8 tactics are in #57842. Neither is included in this fusion PR.\n\n## Communication choice and token cutoff\n\nKeep multicast and the 16-token cutoff. A controlled GB200 TP4 experiment replaced multicast stores with explicit stores to each of the four peers, retaining the same math, Lamport synchronization, cleanup, and PDL. Push did not consistently improve performance:\n\n| Tokens | Multicast kernel | Push kernel | Multicast model forward | Push model forward |\n| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |\n| 1 | 14.348 \u00b5s | 14.634 \u00b5s | 4.054 ms | 4.060 ms |\n| 8 | 14.395 \u00b5s | 14.972 \u00b5s | 5.724 ms | 5.728 ms |\n| 16 | 13.910 \u00b5s | 15.795 \u00b5s | 7.133 ms | 7.130 ms |\n\nKernel timings use cold-L2 CUDA-graph replay, five samples of 50 replays, and the maximum rank time. Model timings use the same synthetic-weight model instance, KV8704, identical tactics, and three samples of 20 replays; they exclude the output head and serving. Multicast and push model outputs were byte-identical on every rank at all nine tested sizes (1\u2013128).\n\nExtending fusion to 24, 32, 48, 64, 96, and 128 tokens regressed model-forward time in this screen, despite isolated kernel gains; coefficient overlap remained disabled above 16. Some nonstandard sizes used default tactics because exact cache buckets were absent. A follow-up using normal serving autotune buckets confirmed the gain at 1 and 16 tokens (4.667\u21924.060 ms and 7.783\u21927.127 ms). Near-boundary runs at 17 and 20 tokens failed the unfused baseline's native-top-k correctness check, so no timings from those shapes are accepted. This supports retaining 16 conservatively; it does not establish the exact crossover. No new model accuracy evaluation was run for the experimental variants.\n\nMulticast requires a supported NVLink/NVSwitch configuration and successful group memory setup; GPU generation alone does not establish support. Explicit peer stores could broaden support to Hopper-or-newer systems with suitable peer-memory access without multicast. That would require separate allocation/dispatch support and hardware validation: this PR remains SM100 TP4, and the experimental push variant reused the existing workspace. Push is a possible portability fallback, not a demonstrated GB200 performance improvement.\n\n## Latest model-forward comparison against main\n\nMeasured candidate `dd63c1fa00` (runtime source identical to the subsequently merged PR head `7be123b000`) versus main `d2983f2f16` fetched at benchmark start, including merged overlap and the latest DSpark block-table fix in both arms. "source": "github", "kind": "pr", "url": "https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/42864", "title": "[Perf] dsv41: Speed up decode-size mHC mixing with a vectorized split-K reduce and 160 K slices on SM120", "body": "## Motivation\n\n`hc_mix_stats_sinkhorn` is the CUDA Triton path for DeepSeek-V4.x mHC mixing statistics and Sinkhorn, run twice per layer. It is used at every row count on SM120, on SM100 when the DeepGEMM prenorm GEMM is not used (including below 128 rows), and on SM90 at one row. It has two launches:\n\n1. `_hc_mix_stats_partial_kernel`: one CTA per (row tile, K slice). K=20480 is split into 80 slices.\n2. `_hc_mix_reduce_sinkhorn_kernel`: one single-warp CTA per row, which adds the 80 slice partials in a serial `static_range` loop before the Sinkhorn.\n\nAt decode sizes the serial loop takes about as long as the partial kernel. With one row tile, 80 CTAs also occupy fewer than half of the 188 SMs on an RTX PRO 6000.\n\n## Modifications\n\n- `_hc_mix_reduce_sinkhorn_vec_kernel`: loads the partials as one `[slices, cols]` tile and reduces them with `tl.sum`, then runs the unchanged Sinkhorn. There is still one CTA per row, and the reduction tree depends only on the slice count, so results are deterministic and batch-invariant. The summation order differs from the serial loop. `hc_mix_stats_sinkhorn` uses it on SM120 (compute capability 12.0), where it was measured; other GPUs keep the serial reducer, so their results are unchanged. The bf16x3 and DeepGEMM paths keep the serial reducer with 16 slices; DeepGEMM also keeps its residual input.\n- `hc_mix_stats_sinkhorn(..., decode=False)`: with `decode=True` on SM120 (compute capability 12.0 only), it splits K into 160 slices when the number of 64-wide K blocks is a multiple of 160. `DeepseekV4DecoderLayer.forward_hc_pre_from_prev` sets `decode` for decode/idle and target-verify forward passes and passes it through `mhc.run_attn_post` / `run_moe_post`, `_compute_triplet`, `mix_stats` and `_mix_stats_impl` to `hc_mix_stats_sinkhorn`. Each new `decode` parameter defaults to False. Prefill/extend, other callers (including the DSpark draft layer, which calls `mix_stats` directly), other GPUs, and the unfused `hc_mix_stats` keep the existing choice (80 for K=20480). The slice count depends on K, the device, and the forward mode, never on M. A row therefore gets the same bits at any batch size within decode/verify on this backend, and likewise within prefill. A decode row can also run beside prefill rows in a MIXED batch, which takes the prefill split, so with batch-invariant mode enabled (`--enable-deterministic-inference`) `_mix_stats_impl` passes `decode=False` in every mode, as it already disables the compensated projections in that mode.\n\n## Accuracy Tests\n\nNew `test_hc_mix_stats_sinkhorn.py` (GPU) and `test_deepseek_v4_mhc_decode_split.py` (CPU). With this branch head's `mhc.py` and tests, all 23 tests in `test_hc_mix_stats_sinkhorn.py` passed on an RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell (SM120), and the 4 tests in `test_deepseek_v4_mhc_decode_split.py` passed on CPU. I have not run the ported model code end to end on a GPU (`deepseek_v4.py`, `deepseek_v4_mhc.py` on current main). The tests cover:\n- Slice selection: 160 for decode and 80 for prefill on SM120; 80 for both on SM100 and SM121; 80 for a K whose 64-wide block count is not a multiple of 160.\n- Accuracy: K=20480 in decode mode at M = 1, 6, 48 and 300 (160 slices) and in prefill mode at M = 6 and 300 (80 slices), plus K = 5120, 4096 and 192 (80, 64 and 1 slices). The fused op matches the unfused `hc_mix_stats` (serial sum, 80 slices at K=20480) followed by the Sinkhorn within rtol 1e-5 / atol 1e-6. It also matches FP64 mixing statistics followed by the FP32 Sinkhorn within rtol 1e-4 / atol 1e-5.\n- Determinism and batch invariance in each mode, with the device forced to SM120 (vectorized reduce) and to SM100 (serial reduce) on any host GPU, as in the accuracy cases. The test checks the selected reducer and slice count, that repeated calls are bitwise equal, and that rows computed alone, as the first 8, 9, 2048 and 2049, and as every 7th of a 2056-row batch are bitwise equal to the same rows in that batch. These subsets use all three row tiles (8, 16 and 32 rows; 32 starts at 2049 rows).\n- Model wiring, on CPU with a mocked layer and no weights: the real `forward_hc_pre_from_prev`, posts and `mix_stats` pass `decode=True` to `hc_mix_stats_sinkhorn` for both hyper-connections in decode, idle and target-verify forward passes, and `decode=False` in extend, mixed, draft-extend and split-prefill passes. With batch-invariant mode enabled, every forward mode passes `decode=False`, so decode and MIXED batches select the same slice count (80 on SM120). A direct `mix_stats` call defaults to `decode=False`.\n\n## Speed Tests and Profiling\n\nPer call (partial + reduce/Sinkhorn, `us`) on one RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Max-Q Workstation Edition (SM120, 188 SMs, 250 W power limit, used only by the benchmark), torch 2.14.1+cu130, Triton 3.8.0. Inputs are BF16 `[M, 20480]`. Each CUDA graph covers 24 distinct `[24, 20480]` FP32 weights at M <= 64 and 4 weights above; the time is the best of 20 graph replays divided by the number of calls. This is the commit half of tree-structured speculative decoding for GDN; #6155 is the verify half. The two are independent kernels and merge in either order, but an engine needs both to run a tree.\n\nTree speculative decoding (EAGLE-2/3 with `topk > 1`) accepts a path through the draft that in general is not a prefix: with three draft tokens a request may accept `{0, 2}` and reject the sibling at row 1. `accept_lens` is a count and cannot express that, and the commit kernel replays rows `0..n-1` by loop counter, so the rejected row reaches the checkpoint. That is measured, not inferred: poisoning row 1 with NaN and asking for three accepted tokens NaNs 100% of the committed state on `main`.\n\nThe recurrence is path-agnostic. Both folds build the Gram matrix and the coefficient recurrence over staged positions, not cache rows, so an ordered path keeps the strictly-triangular structure and only the load index moves. The change is four load sites in the SIMT fold and three in the tcgen05 fold. `accept_paths=None` compiles a `HAS_PATHS=False` variant with no gather, which is bitwise identical to the kernel before this PR, so chain decoding pays nothing. `accept_lens` is retained as that chain fast path, and `row j` of request `i` is read only when `j < accept_lens[i]`.\n\nOut-of-range rows are clamped into `[0, T)` rather than rejected, because checking values on the host would need a device synchronization. `track_steps` needs no change: it already counts positions along the accepted sequence, which is what a path replays. The fp64 reference in `flashinfer/trace/templates/gdn.py` gains the same argument.\n\nSecond commit: tracked commits run on the tcgen05 fold. Until now any commit with `track_state_indices` fell back to the FP32 SIMT fold, and SGLang's `extra_buffer` mamba radix strategy passes track tensors on every commit, so in practice every commit under that strategy took the slower kernel, 20 to 25 percent slower at the shapes the all-layer commit runs at. The SIMT fold gains a `TRACK_ONLY` constexpr: a row with a live track slot and an in-range step replays only up to that step and writes only the track slot, every other CTA exits at the top. When tracking is requested the dispatcher runs that pass first, against the untouched checkpoint, then the tcgen05 fold commits the live slots as before; the ordering is what makes it correct. Below B x HV of about 256 the extra launch costs more than it saves, so `backend=\"auto\"` keeps SIMT for tracked commits there; explicit `tcgen05` always takes the new path.\n\nAll 36 layers in one launch on B200, CUDA-graph timed, in microseconds:\n\n| B | HV | slots | old tracked commit (SIMT) | new tracked commit (snapshot pass + tcgen05 fold) |\n|---|---|---|---|---|\n| 13 | 32 | 66 | 506 | 458 |\n| 21 | 32 | 106 | 770 | 729 |\n| 32 | 32 | 106 | 1281 | 1115 |\n| 64 | 8 | 1036 | 613 | 569 |\n| 32 | 8 | 1036 | 297 | 290 |\n| 8 | 8 | 1036 | 68 | 80 |\n\nStacked on #6229, which touches the same validation block. "https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/45207", "title": "[Spec] DSPARK: hand the overlap readback a snapshot of the folded accept, not views (#42465)", "body": "## Motivation\r\n\r\n#42465: DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash with `--speculative-algorithm DSPARK` and HiCache `write_through` deadlocks across TP ranks. With `SGLANG_ENABLE_RANK_CONSENSUS_CHECKER=1` the ranks diverge on `cache_finished_req ... owned_kv_len` by 1-2 tokens, so each rank inserts a different prefix and the write-through backups no longer line up.\r\n\r\nThe mechanism, as @divyvasal found: the folded accept runs inside the target-verify CUDA graph and writes fixed epilogue buffers (`commit_lens_buf`, `out_tokens_buf`, ...) that the next replay rewrites. `accept_and_finalize(folded_accept=True)` returned `read_accept(bs)`, i.e. views of those buffers, and the DSPARK worker put them into `GenerationBatchResult.accept_lens` / `next_token_ids`. Under the overlap scheduler `_copy_result_to_cpu` issues that readback on `copy_stream` after `copy_stream.wait_stream(forward_stream)` and then launches forward N+1 without waiting for the copy. When the copy engine is busy, for example behind the write-through device-to-host copy of a ~540K-token prefix, the readback runs after replay N+1 and reads step N+1's accept lengths. Each rank races on its own, so ranks commit different token counts. The in-graph accept is broadcast from rank 0, so the ranks agree on the device; only the host readback diverges.\r\n\r\n## Modifications\r\n\r\n- `dspark_verify.py`: `DsparkVerifyEpilogue.snapshot_accept(bs)` returns clones of the six accept buffers. The clones are made on the forward stream right after the replay, so stream order pins them to step N, and `async_d2h`'s `record_stream` keeps them alive until the readback has run. `TargetVerifyExecutor.accept_and_finalize` returns the snapshot on the folded path. `read_accept` keeps returning views, because the in-graph `_accept` writes through them (`build_accept_outs(..., out=self.read_accept(bs))`).\r\n- `scheduler.py`: comment in `_copy_result_to_cpu` updated; no behavior change (the DSpark inline copy under Confidential Computing is kept as validated).\r\n- Cost: six small device-to-device copies per verify step on the forward stream, no extra stream sync.\r\n\r\n### Relation to #42812\r\n\r\n#42812 clones inside `read_accept`. That was right at its base (264d1c20, 2026-10-06), where `_accept` wrote the buffers directly. Since #43790 (2026-10-12) `_accept` passes `read_accept(bs)` as its in-graph destination, so cloning there makes the graph write into throwaway clones and the static buffers never update. On today's main the existing `test_dspark_accept_tail.py::test_graph_accept_matches_eager_greedy` fails with #42812's hunk applied (4 subtests). This PR keeps the alias where the graph needs it and snapshots where the views escape. @shanemort1982 reported the same breakage on #42812 on 2026-10-19 and proposed the same split (views accessor as the write target, clones for the reader); this PR keeps `read_accept` as the views so the in-graph call site is unchanged and adds `snapshot_accept` for the reader.\r\n\r\n## Accuracy / tests\r\n\r\n- `test/registered/unit/spec/test_dspark_accept_tail.py::TestFoldedAcceptSnapshot` (CPU): the folded `accept_and_finalize` output must not alias the epilogue buffers and must keep its values after the buffers are rewritten. Fails on main (`AssertionError: True is not false : correct_len`), passes with the fix. The existing parity case still passes.\r\n- `test/registered/unit/spec/test_dspark_overlap_readback_streams.py` (1-GPU): deterministic replay of the interleaving with real streams and `async_d2h`: a spin kernel on copy_stream stands in for the busy copy engine, forward_stream rewrites the buffers for step N+1; views read step N+1 (the hazard), the snapshot reads step N. On an H200 (main 5cbe2371a5 + this change): both cases pass; against the pre-fix `dspark_verify.py` the view case still reproduces the hazard and the snapshot case fails. The full `test/registered/unit/spec/` sweep passes (308 tests, 176 subtests). Re-run on 2026-10-19 against main 8e7601ae4a: same outcomes, sweep 311 passed, 182 subtests.\r\n- Not reproduced end to end: the hang needs DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash on 4 GPUs (TP4); @divyvasal validated the equivalent clone at 43.1M tokens per replica with 0 rank divergence in #42812.\r\n\r\n## Checklist\r\n\r\n- [x] Format your code according to the [Format code with pre-commit](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#format-code-with-pre-commit).\r\n- [x] Add unit tests according to the [Run and add unit tests](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#run-and-add-unit-tests).\r\n- [ ] Update documentation: not applicable.\r\n- [ ] Provide accuracy and speed benchmark results: not applicable (no numerics change; six tiny D2D copies per verify step).\r\n- [x] Follow the SGLang code style [guidance](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#code-style-guidance).\r\n", "created_at": "2026-10-19T17:15:10Z", "updated_at": "2026-10-20T08:06:45Z", "fetched_at": "2026-10-20T12:18:51Z", "state": "open", "merged_at": null, "parent": null, "tags": ["deepseek-v4.1-flash", "deepseek", "speculation"], "metadata": {"number": 45207, "labels": [], "comments": 1, "state_reason": null}, "content_hash": "9bcfe2a6b1e61749cb0f2c7d3f6236801d4a9283172c7b50082731df4895de43", "rank": -9.136642318477584}, {"id": "github:sgl-project/sglang:45093", "source": "github", "kind": "pr", "url": "https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/45093", "title": "[Feat] volundr: Add Agens Volundr model support", "body": "## Motivation\n\nAgens Volundr (`Blockway/Agens-Volundr-32B-v1`, `Blockway/Agens-Volundr-32B-v1-INT4` (W4A16)) is a hybrid model that\ntoday only runs from a patched SGLang build (`ghcr.io/blockwayz/agens-sglang:v1-sm89` / `v1-sm90`). The indexer key\n  depends on the layer input, so each BCSA layer keeps a per-token side cache indexed by\n  `out_cache_loc` like K/V. One `attn` layer is plain dense attention.\n- **mHC** (manifold hyper-connections): 4 residual streams with Sinkhorn-normalised mixing around\n  every layer.\n- **Engram**: hashed n-gram memory on two layers; needs the two previous token ids of every token.\n- Optional vision tower: SGLang's qwen3_vl vision model and MRoPE, unchanged.\n\nThe layer map comes from `config.mixer_types`; the attention layers do not sit on a fixed interval.\n\n## Modifications\n\nNew files\n\n- `srt/models/volundr.py` \u2014 `VolundrForCausalLM`, `VolundrForConditionalGeneration`. Every attention/MLP RMSNorm is the zero-centred\n  `GemmaRMSNorm`; mHC and the KDA output norm are plain.\n- `srt/configs/volundr.py` \u2014 `VolundrTextConfig` (layer map from `mixer_types`, KDA state layout via\n  `KimiLinearCacheParams`, BCSA/Engram/mHC fields with defaults), `VolundrConfig` (vision + text);\n  registered in `_CONFIG_REGISTRY` and the linear-attention model registry (-> `KDAAttnBackend`).\n- `kernels/ops/layernorm/volundr_mhc.py`, `kernels/ops/attention/volundr_bcsa.py` \u2014 Triton kernels for\n  mHC mix/combine and the BCSA decode block-key write / far branch (~6,000 small launches per decode\n  step become a few per layer). Manifold-Constrained HC (mHC) stabilizes this formulation at scale. The large gains from N{=}1 to N{=}4 suggest residual-stream expansion as a promising scaling axis. However, existing HC-family methods typically stop at N{=}4. Our experiments reveal why: scaling mHC beyond this point yields diminishing performance gains and rapidly increasing training cost. We attribute this limitation to two bottlenecks: insufficient write-back information for an expanding number of streams and residual-mixing generation whose cost scales cubically with N. To address both bottlenecks, we propose xHC (Expanded Hyper-Connections), the first HC-family method to achieve meaningful expansion beyond N{=}4. xHC combines temporal feature augmentation for richer write-back with a sparse residual-stream architecture that updates only k=4 of the N=16 streams while retaining dense access to the full residual state. Across 18B and 28B MoE models, xHC delivers strong and consistent downstream improvements. On an 18B MoE model, xHC improves the average downstream score by 4.0 points over mHC, while adding only modest training FLOPs over the vanilla baseline. Scaling-law experiments show that the vanilla and mHC require 1.50times and 1.19times the compute of xHC, respectively, to reach the same loss. Practical large-N training also requires controlling memory traffic from the expanded residual state. When\nr != p\n, it generally does not.\nA minimal non-degenerate example demonstrates the final marginal bias:\np = [0.3, 0.7]\nr = [0.30078125, 0.69921875]\nq = [0.4, 0.6]\n\na = [1, 0.6 / 0.7]\nc = [1, 0]\n\nPr[out = 0] = 0.30078125 + 0.69921875 * (1 - 0.6 / 0.7)\n            = 0.40066964\nq[0]        = 0.40000000\nThe exact bf16 error bound is not the important part of the fix, but the scale is enough to matter: bf16 has 7 explicit mantissa bits, spacing near 1 of\n2^-7 ~= 0.78%\n, and round-to-nearest error on the order of\n2^-8 ~= 0.39%\nfor normal-range values.\nThis PR changes\nsample_tokens\nto cast before temperature scaling and softmax:\nflat_logits\n=\nlogits\n.\nreshape\n(\n-\n1\n,\nvocab_size\n).\nfloat\n()\n/\ntemperature\nThat makes the sampled draft distribution match the\np\nused by rejection sampling.\n2. The candidate is rebased onto main `2528cd2b91`, including CI maintenance base `ff8d964cf5b6`.\r\n\r\n## Motivation\r\n\r\n`--moe-a2a-backend flashinfer_megamoe` currently requires SM100. FlashInfer #6346 added `sm120_mxfp4_mxfp8_bf16_cake`, a fused EP all-to-all + MXFP4 x MXFP8 expert-compute kernel for SM120 (RTX PRO Blackwell) that runs through the same `flashinfer.moe_ep.MoEEpMegaLayer` API this backend already uses. This PR wires it into the existing `flashinfer_megamoe` path for FP4-expert checkpoints, starting with DeepSeek-V4-Flash.\r\n\r\nThe kernel targets **prefill**. On 4x RTX PRO 5000 Blackwell (72 GB, PCIe) it roughly doubles prefill throughput over `--moe-runner-backend flashinfer_mxfp4` at the same TP4 / attention-DP4 layout, while decode with a few requests per rank is slower (numbers below). The recommended use is the prefill server of a PD-disaggregated deployment, with decode on the existing SM120 recipe; the server logs this at startup when it is not a PD prefill server.\r\n\r\nThe PR also fixes a static-EPLB bug on DeepSeek's `forward_normal` path, which serves `flashinfer_megamoe` (SM100 included) and the plain TP MoE: it only mapped logical to physical expert ids with `--enable-eplb`, so `--init-expert-location` alone (which also selects a dispatch algorithm) left the router's logical ids pointing at the physical layout the weights were loaded in.\r\n\r\n## Modifications\r\n\r\n1. **[Fix] `models/deepseek_v2.py`**: `DeepseekV2MoE._normal_path_dispatch_info()` always builds `ExpertLocationDispatchInfo` on non-NextN layers, as the DeepEP path already does. `init_new` returns `None` without a dispatch algorithm, so the default path is unchanged.\r\n2. **SM120 branch of `flashinfer_megamoe`** (`layers/moe/flashinfer_megamoe.py`, `arg_groups/moe_hook.py`, `environ.py`):\r\n   - Platform gate: SM120 with compute capability exactly 12.0, FP4 experts, EP >= 2, and a FlashInfer build exporting `Sm120_Mxfp4_Mxfp8_Bf16_Cake_MegaMoeConfig` (clear error otherwise). `--enable-eplb` is rejected (the packed scales are not expert-major); speculative decoding without an explicit `--speculative-moe-runner-backend` is rejected (the default draft runner `flashinfer_trtllm` is SM100-only). Settings the SM120 kernel cannot honor fail at startup instead of after the model loads: an unknown transport table, `NCCL_CUMEM_ENABLE=0`, the SM100-only `SGLANG_FLASHINFER_MEGAMOE_COMBINE_DTYPE` / `..._IN_KERNEL_FC2_REDUCE`, and a per-rank prefill chunk or CUDA-graph batch larger than the workspace (`validate_flashinfer_megamoe_sm120_token_budget`). SM100 behaviour is unchanged.\r\n   - `NCCL_CUMEM_ENABLE=1` by default on this path: the kernel joins the EP group's NCCL communicator through NCCL's Device API, which needs cuMem buffers (SGLang otherwise sets it to 0). Same pattern as the `deepep_v2` branch.\r\n   - Weights: FlashInfer's own preprocessing (`preprocess_sm120_mxfp4_mxfp8_cake_mega_weights`). FC1 is a gate/up row interleave of `w13` and is written back into `w13`; FC1/FC2 alias the layer weights, so the experts stay resident once. The float32 (E8M0-widened) checkpoint scales are converted exactly to UE8M0 bytes and replaced by the packed kernel scales.\r\n   - Forward: one pooled workspace; each call stages However, training and deploying such models incur substantial computational and memory costs, motivating the development of low-precision training techniques. Recent work has demonstrated that 4-bit floating-point (FP4) formats--such as MXFP4 and NVFP4--can be successfully applied to linear GEMM operations in large language models (LLMs), achieving up to 4x improvements in compute throughput and memory efficiency compared to higher-precision baselines. In this work, we investigate the recently proposed HiFloat4 FP4 format for Huawei Ascend NPUs and systematically compare it with MXFP4 in large-scale training settings. All experiments are conducted on Ascend NPU clusters, with linear and expert GEMM operations performed entirely in FP4 precision.
